title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS IF JESUS NEVER COMMANDED IT? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE DECEMBER 25 FOREVER
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS CELEBRATE CHRISTMAS IF JESUS NEVER COMMANDED IT? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT COULD CHANGE HOW YOU SEE DECEMBER 25 FOREVER

What if the greatest danger isn't celebrating a day Jesus never commanded—but allowing a celebration about Jesus to become a substitute for actually following Him? Before you defend Christmas or condemn it, there is something in Scripture every Christian needs to confront.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.

Not before your pastor. Not before your denomination. Not before the Christians arguing on Facebook about Christmas trees, December 25, pagan traditions, and whether genuine believers should celebrate the birth of the Savior.
Before Jesus Himself.
And imagine Him asking you something you never expected.
Not, "Did you put up a Christmas tree?"
Not, "Did you refuse to celebrate December 25?"
But something far more personal.
"Did you love Me? Did you obey My Word? Did you honor Me with the freedom I gave you? And how did you treat the brothers and sisters who reached a different conclusion?"
Suddenly, the argument looks different.

Because somewhere between the Christmas decorations and the heated theological debates, between the families gathering around dinner tables and the Christians accusing one another of compromise, we may have forgotten the Person at the center of the conversation.
Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God.
The Word who became flesh.
The Savior who entered a world drowning in sin, not to decorate our traditions, but to redeem our souls.
And here is the question we cannot afford to avoid:
If the Bible never commands Christians to celebrate Christmas, should we celebrate it at all?
The answer may challenge both those who love Christmas and those who reject it.
Because Scripture gives us something more demanding than a simple yes or no.
It calls us to truth, conscience, holiness, love, and the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable discovery is this:
You can celebrate Christmas and dishonor Christ.
You can refuse to celebrate Christmas and still dishonor Christ.
And you can do either one with a sincere desire to obey God.
That is why this conversation matters.
Not because December 25 determines our salvation.
But because what we do with our convictions reveals something about our relationship with the One who saved us.
Let's begin where every Christian conversation should begin.
With Scripture.
The Bible never commands the Church to observe an annual festival commemorating the birth of Jesus Christ.
There is no New Testament instruction establishing December 25 as His birthday.
No apostolic command requiring Christmas services.
No biblical calendar identifying a day on which all believers must celebrate the incarnation.
That is not an attack on Christmas.
It is simply a fact we must acknowledge if we claim to honor the authority of God's Word.
Jesus explicitly instructed His disciples to remember His sacrificial death through the Lord's Supper.
In Luke 22:19, He said:
"this do in remembrance of me." (KJV)
But no comparable command establishes an annual celebration of His birth.
Does that automatically make Christmas sinful?
Not necessarily.
And this is where the discussion becomes more profound than many people realize.
The absence of a biblical command does not automatically establish a biblical prohibition.
But neither does the absence of a prohibition give us permission to turn human traditions into divine commandments.
Those two truths must remain together.
Because the moment we separate them, we risk either binding consciences where God has not bound them or excusing practices that Scripture actually condemns.
The apostle Paul addressed a remarkably similar problem among early Christians.
Some believers considered particular days more significant than others. Others regarded all days alike.
And Paul's response was not to declare that every believer must observe the same calendar.
Romans 14:5–6 says:
"One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord..." (KJV)
Read that slowly.
"Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind."
The original Greek expression is:
ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω
Hekastos en tō idiō noi plērophoreisthō.
A faithful rendering is:
"Let each person be fully convinced in his own mind."
The Greek verb plērophoreisthō communicates being fully assured or convinced.
Paul was not encouraging careless religious experimentation.
He was calling believers to act from sincere, informed conviction before God.

The immediate context concerns disputed practices, including the observance of days and questions about food. Paul was not specifically discussing Christmas, which was not established as a Christian annual festival in his time.
But the principle matters.
Where God has not commanded a universal religious observance, Christians must be careful not to manufacture one.
And where Scripture permits genuine differences of conscience, Christians must be equally careful not to condemn one another over matters God has not made tests of faithfulness.
Now imagine two believers.
One gathers with family on December 25, reads Luke chapter 2, sings hymns about Christ's incarnation, feeds struggling neighbors, and thanks God for sending His Son.
Another believer chooses not to observe Christmas because of concerns about historical traditions, commercialization, or the absence of a biblical command.
Both desire to honor Jesus.
Both are seeking to obey Scripture.
Must one automatically be condemned?
Romans 14 gives us strong reasons to answer no, provided neither is participating in something Scripture actually forbids.
Paul continues in Romans 14:4:
"Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth." (KJV)
That should make us uncomfortable.
Because sometimes Christians are more eager to win an argument about a holiday than to demonstrate the humility of the Savior they claim to represent.
We can spend hours exposing someone else's Christmas decorations while ignoring the bitterness growing inside our own hearts.
We can become experts at identifying questionable traditions while remaining strangers to mercy.
And Jesus never told us that winning religious arguments would be the identifying mark of His disciples.
He said in John 13:35:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
But there is another side to this conversation.
One we must not ignore.
Some Christians ask:
"What about the pagan origins of Christmas?"
That question deserves a thoughtful answer, not ridicule.
December 25 was not identified as Jesus' birthday in the New Testament.
The historical development of Christmas involved the Christian calendar of the late Roman world, and scholars have debated why December 25 became prominent.
Some historical explanations emphasize the relationship between Christmas and Roman winter festivals or solar symbolism.
Others emphasize early Christian chronological calculations connecting the date of Jesus' conception with the date of His death, leading to a birth date nine months later.
The surviving historical evidence does not establish one universally accepted explanation.
It is therefore misleading to claim with certainty that Christmas was simply copied wholesale from a pagan festival.
It is also misleading to pretend that every Christmas custom originated directly from Scripture.
Neither claim does justice to history.
Certain modern Christmas customs developed over many centuries, across different cultures, with religious, seasonal, and commercial influences.
And yes, some practices have associations that deserve examination.
But here is the critical biblical distinction.
A historical association does not, by itself, settle whether every present-day use of a custom constitutes idolatry.
Scripture evaluates worship, allegiance, intention, and conduct.
That does not mean origins are irrelevant.
It means we must examine them carefully rather than treating every resemblance as proof of identical religious meaning.
Consider Jeremiah 10.
This passage is frequently quoted in arguments against Christmas trees.
Jeremiah 10:3–4 describes a tree cut from the forest, worked by a craftsman, and decorated with silver and gold.
At first glance, someone may say:
"That sounds exactly like a Christmas tree!"
But continue reading.
Jeremiah 10:5 describes the objects as unable to speak or walk.
And the surrounding passage repeatedly contrasts lifeless idols with the living God.
The context concerns the manufacture and worship of idols.
It is not a direct prophecy about modern Christmas decorations.
To use the passage responsibly, we must recognize what Jeremiah was actually condemning.
Idolatry.
The creation of religious objects that people treat as gods.
A decorated tree in a living room is not automatically an idol.
But if anything becomes an object of worship, superstition, or misplaced devotion, the biblical warning against idolatry absolutely applies.
And that includes more than trees.
Money can become an idol.
Family traditions can become idols.
Religious pride can become an idol.
Even our determination to prove that we are more biblically faithful than other Christians can become a source of sinful self-exaltation.
That is the part of the conversation few people want to discuss.
Because it is much easier to inspect somebody else's decorations than to inspect our own hearts.
Yet the Bible never asks us to choose between truth and humility.
It commands both.
Now consider Deuteronomy 12:30–31, where God warned Israel not to inquire how the surrounding nations worshiped their gods and then imitate those practices in worshiping Him.
That warning is serious.
God does not accept idolatrous worship simply because someone attaches His name to it.
Christians should never use Christmas—or any other occasion—as an excuse for occult practices, false worship, greed, drunkenness, dishonesty, or disobedience.
But we must also respect the historical and covenantal context of Deuteronomy and distinguish actual imitation of idolatrous worship from practices whose present meaning is not inherently religious.
Otherwise, we risk making accusations Scripture itself does not establish.
Jesus warned against another danger in Mark 7:8:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men..." (KJV)
Notice what makes the tradition dangerous.
It displaces God's commandment.
A tradition becomes spiritually destructive when we elevate it above Scripture, treat it as necessary for salvation, or use it to excuse disobedience.
Christmas is not a sacrament commanded by Christ.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It is not proof that someone is spiritually mature.
And refusing to celebrate it is not automatic proof of greater holiness.
No human tradition should be allowed to sit on the throne that belongs to Jesus alone.
But now we need to go somewhere even deeper.
Beyond the calendar.
Beyond history.
Beyond trees, gifts, candles, and Christmas songs.
We need to talk about the Child whose birth Christians are remembering.
Because although Scripture does not command an annual Christmas celebration, it does proclaim the incarnation as an astonishing act of divine grace.
John 1:14 declares:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us..." (KJV)
The original Greek begins:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
"And the Word became flesh."
Those words should stop us in our tracks.
Logos—the Word.
Sarx—flesh.
Egeneto—became.
John was not describing a mere moral teacher entering human history.
He was proclaiming that the eternal Word, who was with God and was God according to John 1:1, truly became human.
Without ceasing to be divine.
The Son of God entered the human condition.
He knew hunger.
He knew exhaustion.
He experienced sorrow.
He wept.
He endured rejection.
He suffered.
And He did it without sin.
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world He had made.
Not because humanity deserved a Savior.
But because God is rich in mercy.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes personal.
Because there are people reading this who have spent years feeling disqualified from God's love.
People who have destroyed relationships.
People carrying private addictions.
People who still remember the face of someone they hurt.
People who have prayed for forgiveness and then wondered whether God could possibly mean it when He promises mercy.
People who sit in church looking perfectly composed while silently fighting battles nobody knows exist.
And somewhere in the middle of this debate about Christmas, we need to remember why Jesus came.
He did not enter the world because humanity had successfully made itself holy.
He came because sinners needed redemption.
Matthew 1:21 records the angel's words to Joseph:
"thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." (KJV)
In Greek, the name appears as:
Ἰησοῦς — Iēsous
This Greek form corresponds to the Hebrew/Aramaic name commonly rendered Yeshua, related to the Hebrew name Yehoshua, expressing the idea that the LORD saves.
The angel did not say He would merely inspire His people.
Or entertain them.
Or give them a beautiful religious season.
"He shall save his people from their sins."
That is the center.
Not the date.
Not the decorations.
Not the gifts.
Salvation.
The holy God rescuing guilty humanity through His Son.
And the birth of Jesus cannot be understood apart from His cross.
The manger points toward Calvary.
The Child was born to live in perfect obedience, to give His life as a ransom, and to rise victorious over death.
The wood of a manger did not save us.
The wooden cross was not magical either.
It was the crucified and risen Christ—His person and His redeeming work—who accomplished our salvation.
And this is why the Gospel is more than a heartwarming Christmas story.
It is a declaration that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new through Jesus Christ.
Maybe your life has become a scandal.
Maybe people remember the worst thing you ever did.
Maybe your family still talks about your failures.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun a past that follows you into every quiet moment.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your public reputation.
He came to deal with your sin before a holy God.
He calls you to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
And His grace is sufficient to forgive even what you are ashamed to confess.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
Grace.
The Greek word is:
χάρις — charis
Grace, favor, gift.
Not a reward for being religious enough.
Not payment for observing the right holiday.
Not a prize for rejecting the wrong one.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
We do not earn salvation through obedience.
We obey because Christ has saved us and made us His own.
So when we ask whether Christians should celebrate Christmas, perhaps we also need to ask something that reaches beneath the surface.
What kind of life are we living before God during the other 364 days of the year?
Do we speak about the birth of Christ while refusing to forgive someone who wounded us?
Do we sing about peace on earth while cultivating cruelty in our homes?
Do we buy gifts for people we love while ignoring those who cannot afford food?
Do we argue passionately about the pagan origins of Christmas while secretly nurturing lust, envy, hatred, or greed?
Do we call ourselves defenders of biblical truth while refusing to examine whether our own speech reflects the character of Jesus?
The Bible gives us a deeply challenging instruction in 1 Corinthians 10:31:
"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." (KJV)
Whatsoever you do.
That includes December 25.
And December 26.
It includes your family celebrations.
Your decision not to celebrate.
Your social media arguments.
Your purchases.
Your charitable giving.
Your conversations with people who disagree with you.
Every part of life belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
For someone who celebrates Christmas, that means asking whether the celebration genuinely reflects gratitude, love, truth, and holiness.
For someone who abstains, it means asking whether that decision flows from sincere conviction rather than pride, contempt, or a desire to appear superior.
Both must submit to Christ.
And both must be willing to examine themselves.
Because there is a difference between having a biblical conviction and turning that conviction into a weapon against every Christian who disagrees.
Romans 14:10 asks:
"But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother?" (KJV)
That question is painfully relevant.
Imagine a Christian mother who spends Christmas morning reading the Gospel of Luke to her children.
She explains that Jesus is God the Son who became man.
She teaches them that salvation cannot be purchased.
She prays with them.
She invites a lonely neighbor to dinner.
She uses the occasion to speak of the love of God.
Now imagine another Christian family that chooses not to observe Christmas.
Instead, they intentionally teach their children that no particular date has been established by Scripture as Christ's birthday.
They give thanks for the incarnation throughout the year.
They refuse to bind their consciences to a human religious calendar.
They also seek to love their neighbors and proclaim the Gospel.
Which family must God automatically reject?
Scripture gives us no authority to condemn either family merely for those differing practices.
The real questions concern faithfulness to Christ, obedience to His commands, and the condition of the heart.
Of course, sincerity alone does not make every practice acceptable.
A sincerely held belief can still be mistaken.
That is why our consciences must be educated by Scripture.
But Christians must distinguish clear biblical commands from disputable applications.
Otherwise, we create burdens God has not imposed.
Colossians 2:16 says:
"Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:" (KJV)
The context concerns religious regulations and their relationship to Christ, not a direct discussion of modern Christmas celebrations.
Still, the passage reinforces an important truth: believers must not allow human judgment about religious calendars to displace their standing in Christ.
And Romans 14:23 warns that whatever is not from faith is sin.
If you believe celebrating Christmas would violate your conscience before God, do not violate that conscience.
Study Scripture.
Pray.
Seek wise counsel.
Remain teachable.
But do not act against what you sincerely believe God requires.
Likewise, if you celebrate Christmas with a clear conscience, do not use your freedom to mock believers who abstain.
And do not pressure them to participate.
Christian freedom is never permission to disregard Christian love.
There is something profoundly beautiful about believers who can disagree over a nonessential observance without questioning one another's salvation.
Because unity in Christ does not require identical personal traditions.
It requires shared allegiance to the same Lord and submission to the same Gospel.
And perhaps one of the most powerful testimonies the Church could offer during December is not another argument about Christmas.
Perhaps it is a community of believers who actually love one another.
A community where those who celebrate do not ridicule those who abstain.
Where those who abstain do not automatically accuse those who celebrate of idolatry.
Where Scripture is honored.
Where consciences are respected.
Where sin is confronted.
Where grace is proclaimed.
And where Jesus remains greater than every human custom.
Now consider something easily overlooked.
The Bible records extraordinary responses to the birth of Christ.
In Luke 2, the angels announced good news of great joy.
The shepherds went to see the Child and afterward glorified and praised God.
In Matthew 2, the magi came to honor the young Jesus and presented gifts.
These accounts do not establish a command for annual Christmas observance.
But they do show that the arrival of the Messiah was worthy of joy, reverence, and worship.
The shepherds were not celebrating a church holiday.
They were responding to the revelation that the Savior had been born.
And that distinction matters.
We are not commanded to imitate every narrative detail as an annual ritual.
But we are called to worship the Christ whom those narratives reveal.
Luke 2:11 says:
"For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." (KJV)
The Greek title is:
Χριστὸς κύριος — Christos kyrios
"Christ the Lord."
Christos means Anointed One, corresponding to the Hebrew Mashiach, Messiah.
Kyrios means Lord.
This was no ordinary birth announcement.
The promised Messiah had come.
The Savior had entered human history.
And His arrival demanded more than seasonal sentiment.
It demanded recognition of His identity.
Because the baby in Bethlehem is the Lord before whom every knee will bow.
He is not merely a symbol of kindness.
He is not a decoration for a holiday.
He is the crucified, risen, and reigning King.
And He calls us to repentance and faith.
That is why a Christian celebration of Christmas, when freely chosen, should never end with a beautiful manger scene.
It should lead us to the full Gospel.
To the holiness of God.
To the reality of sin.
To the cross of Christ.
To the empty tomb.
To forgiveness.
To discipleship.
To the promise that Jesus will come again.

And if Christmas has become nothing more than expensive gifts, social pressure, exhausting obligations, and religious nostalgia, perhaps we need to ask whether we have lost sight of the One we claim to honor.
You can spend hundreds on presents and still refuse to give someone the apology they deserve.
You can fill your house with lights while allowing resentment to darken your relationships.
You can sing "Joy to the World" while secretly believing your own life is beyond redemption.
You can attend a Christmas service and leave without ever surrendering to the Savior whose birth you just celebrated.
And you can reject every Christmas tradition while still refusing to surrender your pride to Him.
That is why the greatest question is not merely whether you celebrate Christmas.
It is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because there is no saving power in December 25.
There is no saving power in refusing December 25.
There is no saving power in a Christmas tree.
There is no saving power in having no Christmas tree.
There is no saving power in winning a theological argument online.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ alone.
Acts 4:12 declares:
"Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved." (KJV)
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Not another argument.
Not another accusation.
Not another reminder of how badly they have failed.
But the truth that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
You may have walked away from church.
You may have lost confidence in religious leaders.
You may have watched Christians wound one another so deeply that you wondered whether their faith was real.
You may have confused the failures of Christians with the character of Christ.
But please do not let the failures of people keep you from looking honestly at Jesus.
He is not made less holy by our hypocrisy.
His truth does not become false because we sometimes represent it poorly.
His mercy is not exhausted by the sins of those who claim His name.
And His invitation to repent and believe remains.
In John 6:37, Jesus says:
"him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
What a promise.
Not that every sin will be excused without repentance.
Not that following Jesus will cost us nothing.
But that those who truly come to Him will not be turned away.
Perhaps you have been running for years.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind religion.
Perhaps you know how to defend biblical doctrines but have never truly surrendered your life to the Lord those doctrines proclaim.
Or perhaps you are simply exhausted.
Exhausted from pretending to be stronger than you are.
Exhausted from trying to prove your worth.
Exhausted from carrying guilt that never seems to loosen its grip.
The Gospel does not invite you to save yourself through religious performance.
It invites you to come to Christ.
To confess your sin.
To trust in His finished work.
To turn from the darkness and follow the One who is the Light of the world.
And if you already belong to Him, it calls you to keep growing in grace and truth.
That growth includes learning how to handle difficult biblical questions without sacrificing love.
It includes the humility to say, "I may have been wrong."
It includes the courage to say, "Scripture does not command this."
And the wisdom to add, "But Scripture also does not necessarily forbid every voluntary observance of it."
It includes the ability to distinguish between a human custom and an act of idolatry.
Between a personal conviction and a universal command.
Between defending the Gospel and defending our preferences.
And between honoring Christ with a celebration and merely attaching His name to a celebration that has no meaningful place for Him.
So should Christians celebrate Christmas?
Christians are not biblically required to celebrate Christmas, and they are not automatically sinning by choosing to celebrate it.
A believer may set aside a day to remember Christ's birth, provided the observance is consistent with Scripture, free from idolatry, and offered sincerely to the glory of God.
Another believer may abstain out of conscience and devotion to biblical authority.
Neither practice should be imposed as a condition of salvation or as a universal test of spiritual maturity.
But both believers are commanded to love God, obey Christ, reject idolatry, speak truth, and love one another.
And that is where the real test begins.
Not with a date on a calendar.
But with the heart that approaches it.
If you celebrate, celebrate with truth.
If you abstain, abstain with humility.
If you disagree, disagree with love.
And whatever you do, do not let a debate about the birth of Jesus distract you from the reason He came.
Because the incarnation is not merely about God entering our world.
It is about God acting in history to accomplish our redemption.
From the manger to the cross.
From the cross to the empty tomb.
From our guilt to His forgiveness.
From spiritual death to new life in Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending our sins never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving those who repent and believe, reconciling them to God, and beginning the transforming work of His grace.
And there is something else I want to say before you leave this article.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read Romans 14 in full.
Read John 1.
Read Luke 2.
Read Colossians 2.
Read Mark 7.
Examine what these passages actually say in context.
Do not simply inherit somebody else's conviction without studying the Word of God.
And do not build your faith on viral arguments, no matter how confident the person speaking may sound.
Build your life on Christ and His Word.
If you are a Christian who celebrates Christmas, I would genuinely love to hear how you seek to keep Jesus at the center.
If you are a Christian who does not celebrate Christmas, I would also love to hear the biblical convictions behind your decision.
And if this article exposed something deeper in your heart—pride, judgment, confusion, spiritual exhaustion, or the need to return to Christ—there is room for that honesty too.
You do not need to pretend to have everything figured out.
We are called to grow in the truth together.
And please, if someone in your life has been wounded by harsh religious arguments, consider sending them this article.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to prove them wrong.
But to invite them back to the heart of the Gospel.
Not because following a page makes anyone a disciple.
But because regular exposure to faithful biblical teaching can encourage us to keep opening the Bible, examining our hearts, and following Jesus in ordinary life.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to help people move beyond shallow religious content into genuine spiritual nourishment, repentance, restoration, and growth in Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, strengthen their families, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
And there is a way you can help this ministry continue reaching people.
Your monthly contribution can be an expression of Christian generosity and a voluntary offering toward Gospel-centered work.
However, I want to be especially clear about something because we have just spent this entire article discussing the danger of turning human practices into divine requirements.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly and without compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Your first allegiance belongs to Jesus Christ, not to any ministry.
It can help us keep teaching.
Keep writing.
Keep making discipleship resources accessible.
Keep reaching people who may never have entered a church but are willing to read one article that points them toward Jesus.
Those products are simply expressions of appreciation and practical resources. They are not spiritual rewards, and purchasing them is never a measure of anyone's faith.
Not everyone can give financially.
But many can pray.
Many can encourage.
Many can share.
Many can invite a friend into a thoughtful conversation about Christ.
And none of those acts should be performed out of guilt or pressure.
They should flow from love.
Because the Gospel we proclaim is not for sale.
The grace of God cannot be purchased.
And Jesus Christ is worthy of our devotion whether we have much to give or almost nothing.
So when December 25 comes, whether you are gathered around a family table or treating it as an ordinary day, remember what matters most.
The Savior has come.
The Word became flesh.
The Son of God lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
He reigns as Lord.
And He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Perhaps you will never look at Christmas quite the same way again.
Perhaps you will celebrate with greater biblical understanding.
Perhaps you will abstain with greater peace.
Perhaps you will finally stop condemning a brother or sister over a matter where Scripture permits differing convictions.
Or perhaps the greatest change will have nothing to do with Christmas at all.
Perhaps you will finally surrender the hidden part of your life that you have been keeping from Christ.
The bitterness.
The guilt.
The pride.
The fear.
The secret sin.
The exhaustion of pretending.
Because in the end, Jesus did not come merely to give humanity a holiday worth celebrating.
He came to save sinners and make them His own.
And that truth is far too glorious to confine to one day of the year.

The greatest tragedy would not be reaching December 25 without a Christmas celebration—but reaching the end of your life having celebrated the birth of Jesus while never surrendering your heart to Him.
